hints.title: Subtract the two integrals
hints.body: For I, put the difference of the integrals into one integral. Then use the given inequality to find the sign of its integrand.
hints.recap: Integrating a nonnegative function from a smaller limit to a larger one gives a nonnegative result.
hints.pitfall: The upper limit can be any nonnegative x.
hints.pause: Decide whether the integral comparison follows.

recall.reminder: Integrating a nonnegative function from a smaller limit to a larger one gives a nonnegative result.

hints.title: Separate height from slope
hints.body: For II, draw a parabola above a horizontal line, with a short downward-sloping tangent somewhere in the allowed interval. Choose equations that make this a valid example.
hints.recap: The height of a curve and its gradient are different quantities.
hints.pitfall: Your example must satisfy the height inequality for every nonnegative input.
hints.pause: Choose simple equations and check their derivatives.

recall.reminder: The height of a curve and its gradient are different quantities.

hints.title: Try parallel lines
hints.body: For III, draw two straight lines with equal gradients and different heights.
hints.recap: Adding a constant changes a graph’s height without changing its derivative.
hints.pitfall: Equal derivatives are allowed by the greater-than-or-equal sign.
hints.pause: Check the hypothesis and conclusion for your lines, then decide which of I, II and III must hold.

recall.reminder: Adding a constant changes a graph’s height without changing its derivative.

solution:
I is true because ∫0xf(t)dt−∫0xg(t)dt=∫0x[f(t)−g(t)]dt≥0 for x≥0.

II is false. Let f(x)=(x−1)2 and g(x)=0. Then f≥g for all x≥0, but f′(0)=−2<0=g′(0).

III is false. Let f(x)=x and g(x)=x+1. Their derivatives are both 1, so the premise holds, yet f(x)<g(x) everywhere.

Answer B: I only.
